params.text: Experiment 3: can a melt emulator trained on 25 cavity runs extrapolate?
Tbot: CDW temperature below the thermocline (°C)
s scales the ice draft; 4 km ISOMIP+ cavity; melt = mean of months 19–24
What each method is tested on
Each fit sees only its training runs; standardisation,
EOFs, kernels and K, n are refitted inside each fold.
in range: leave one run out
Sensitivity repeat: all folds but final without the
5 runs failing N1 (never used for the hypotheses).
Eight ways to predict the melt map
c = ρswcp/(ρiLi); TF: thermal forcing at the ice base
How the predictions are scored (fixed before any fit on real data)
Metrics, per held-out run (Burgard et al. 2022):
• RMSE of the melt map over the run's own ice shelf (Eq. 32)
• relative error of the integrated melt (Eq. 33–34)
• error of the mean melt near the grounding line (Eq. 35)
• M6, M7: spread of the 5 network members; M5–M7: coverage, CRPS
• noise floor: no difference below 0.157 m a-1 or 1.3 % is read
On the 3 final-test runs, the hybrid M7 has a smaller integrated-melt error than M6,
on average and in at least 2 of the 3 runs (a difference below 1.3 % is inconclusive).
Inside the training range (loro), the hybrid costs little: RMSE of M7 ≤ 1.10 × that of M6.
Out of range (zc_out, warm_out, final: 33 cases), the ensemble is never confidently wrong:
no case with spread < 5 % and integrated error > 20 % (Ockenden et al. 2026 replication).
The ranking of all 8 methods is reported as found, whichever wins.
